elements.html:
Between 1961 and 1995 Dieter Rams led design at Braun and set down ten principles for good design. The products were quiet: warm grey housings, one orange control, type set in a geometric sans and nothing that did not need to be there.

A slide can behave the same way. Say the thing once, leave the rest of the surface empty, and put the only colour on the control that matters.

  • Useful before beautiful
  • Unobtrusive, so the content can speak
  • Thorough down to the last detail

elements.html: The SK 4 record player put the turntable under a clear acrylic lid. Critics called it Snow White's coffin. Every competitor copied the lid within a decade.
The same restraint reads as calm on a screen: one typeface, a warm grey ground, and an orange mark that tells you where to look. Everything else is left off.

slides.notes: Headline numbers count up on arrival (fx.countUp). One plain number per box: countUp strips markup and animates every digit it finds. The note at the bottom carries the source or the consequence.

Rams joined Braun in 1955 and became head of design in 1961. The ten principles were first published in the late 1970s and revised through the 1980s.

slides.notes: Chart. Series in charcoal, orange and grey. Bar and line data are plain numbers; only pie takes {name, value}. The legend must be an object to render. textStyle.fontFamily is set so the chart uses Jost rather than the browser default.
Comparison table. Header row in Braun black, 1px hairlines, no zebra. Tables are for specs and comparisons; a numeric trend belongs in the chart layout.

Process. Four numbered knobs joined by a dotted orange track that marches (fx.loop dash-march). In the demo, step 2 is clickable: a transparent rect over it links to a state slide, and the left arrow returns.

Does the product need to exist at all, and for whom.
Remove every part and control that does not earn its place.
Radii, gaps, type and colour, decided once and applied everywhere.
Put it in a home for a month and watch what people actually touch.

elements.html: How a Braun product was designed

Every control is a claim on the user's attention. The SK 4 had a single row of them. The T 3 had one dial and one wheel, and the wheel was the only thing in colour.

Reduction is not minimalism for its own sake: the parts that remain get the whole budget of care.
